newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian minor parties decry lack of poll funds.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian minor parties decry lack of poll funds.

text.p: Indonesia on Friday approved the final list of candidates for the May general elections, but the two legal minority parties complained of a lack of funds for their campaigns.

The list, which will be publicised ahead of the May 29 poll, excludes ousted minority party leader Megawati Sukarnoputri and her supporters and includes three of President Suharto's children as candidates for the ruling Golkar party.

Suharto's eldest daughter, Siti Hardijanti Rukmana, head of construction group Citra Lamtoro Gung, and son Bambang Trihatmodjo, chief of the Bimantara group, ensure Golkar is well-funded as vice-chairman and treasurer, respectively.
Suharto's youngest son, Hutomo Mandala Putra, head of the Humpus group, is also a Golkar candidate.

Interior Minister Yogie Memet, also head of the Indonesian election committee, said the General Election Institute (LPU) had received 150 letters of concern after the temporary list of candidates was circulated nationwide for comment.
But an LPU official said only eight potential candidates for the 425 elected seats in the 500-member national parliament had been withdrawn, including three who had since died.
The other 75 seats are filled by the military, whose members do not vote in the general elections.

However, as the government went through the next step in the formalities ahead of the May 29 poll, leaders of the two legal minority parties complained they did not have enough money to fight effective campaigns.
Tosari Wijaya, secretary-general of the Moslem-orientated United Development Party (PPP), said after the ceremony that the minority parties received most of their funds from the government.

"From the preparation stage until the election is over, we estimate we need four billion rupiah ($1.7 million). If the government wants to only give us one billion, it meets only 25 percent of our needs," Wijaya told reporters.
At the last poll in 1992, the PPP received 250 million rupiah.

Wijaya said donations from party sympathisers, which made up only a minor part of the campaign funding, usually took the form of handing out T-shirts in the party's green colour or hiring vehicles. Foreign donations are illegal.
Surjadi, head of the government-backed faction of the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), said the government was neglecting the needs of the minor parties.

"For 27 provinces, with more than 300 branches and 7,000 sub-districts and 70,000 villages, four billion rupiah is not enough. It is impossible to calculate how much is needed by the party in all regions," Surjadi said.
The minority parties complain that Golkar, whose leaders are government and business figures, is well funded and has easy access to the state-run media.

Golkar won 68 percent of the vote in the last elections in 1992, the PPP 17 percent and the PDI -- now riven by internal disputes -- 15 percent. Golkar is aiming for more than 70 percent in the coming poll.
